train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29539/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [NRP] national. The Polish Government (‘the Government’) were represented by their Agent, Agent, Mr [ PERSON] of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The application was decided on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). The case was quashed and remitted by the Supreme Court. The court awarded the applicant 1,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) (approx. 285 euros (EUR)) in just satisfaction. The court did not examine, however, the period prior to the entry into force of the [DATE_TIME] Act. It referred to the periods [Date_TIME], [Dates] and [DATES] and qualified them as unjustified delays. It also referred to a period of inactivity for which the Łódż Regional Court had been responsible. It found that there had been several periods of unjustified inactivity. The application was dismissed on the grounds of excessive length of the proceedings.

The application was declared partly inadmissible pursuant to Article 35 §§ 3 (a) and 4 of the convention. The applicants are the sons of the late [PERSON] (hereinafter referred to as “Mr [Person]” or “the deceased”) who died in the evening of [DATE_TIME] at his home in [LOCATION], [ LOCATION]. The deceased had regularly been attended at home by his doctor, a General Practitioner. The GP had routinely administered injections of opiates, in particular pethidine at a dosage of 100mg, for pain relief. On several occasions the deceased had recourse to out-of-hours medical services by “Take Care Now” (“TCN”), a private agency. The patient, Mr [PERSON], developed a severe renal colic. His partner contacted the TCN call centre to arrange for an urgent home visit by a doctor. The case was then assigned to doctor [Person], a [NRP] national, who had recently been recruited by TCN through an agency on a self-employed basis to provide out-of-hours care. U. had withdrawn a first application to join Leeds Performers List after being notified that he had not reached a sufficient score in the required English language test. However, the [ LOCATION] and [LOCATION] PCT authorities, unaware that U. was a locum doctor, approved a subsequent application and admitted him to their Performers list. According to an induction report established by a TCN doctor there had not been sufficient time to assess U’s professional competence prior to his first assignment. U. administered 100mg of diamorphine from the respective ampoule included in the palliative care box by intra‑muscular injection. Mr [PERSON]’s partner realised that he was no longer breathing and called an ambulance. On [DATE_TIME] TCN suspended [LOCATION] from duty, terminated his engagement with immediate effect and advised him to return to where he arrived. The GMC suspended the applicant from the [NRP] medical register on an interim basis. U. either received injections of pethidine for acute pain relief or, where the out-of-hours services did not carry pethidine, had been treated with diamorphin. Diamorphine poisoning was the cause of Mr [PERSON]’s death. In a letter of [DATE_TIME] U. apologised for the medical malpractice. He explained that he had confused the opiates and referred to the stress situation he was subject to when making the mistake. He was suspended from the medical register and criminal proceedings were instituted against U. in [LOCATION] and [ LOCATION] The English Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) sent a formal letter of request to the Ministry of Justice of the Land North Rhine‑Westphalia, [LOCation], in accordance with the European Convention on Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters. The request was sent by the German Ministry of Justice. The case is being investigated under Article 152 of the German Code of Criminal Procedure. If found guilty, the defendant could face a prison sentence of up to 10 years. The victim's family have asked that the case be referred to the UK’s Court of Appeal. The prosecution is seeking a restraining order against the defendant. The public has been informed of the case and asked that it be dealt with in line with the law. It is the public interest that this matter is dealt with. The court of appeal has asked that a hearing be held in light of the allegations against the victim. However, the prosecution has declined to make a decision. U. availed himself of his right not to testify. He also declined a subsequent request by the [LOCATION] police to be interviewed in [ LOCATION]. A forensic expert opinion was obtained from a professor of Essen university hospital on the question whether the treatment of the deceased had complied with medical standards. In his final report issued on [DATE_TIME] the expert confirmed that the cause of Mr [PERSON]’s death had been an overdose of diamorphine. The expert concluded that U.’S treatment had thus been inadequate and had violated basic principles of medical care. He pointed out that notwithstanding the fact that the therapeutical use of diam Morphine was in general not permitted in [ Location] and therefore doctors in [LOCation] were as a rule not trained in its use.  Counsel asked for information whether preliminary criminal proceedings were pending against [LOCATION] and, should this be the case, requested access to the relevant investigation files. A draft of the penal order was attached to the application. name: Uli Lutz
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on [DATE_TIME. It originated in an application (no. 9912/82) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State, Mr. [PERSON]. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 2. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, the elected judge of [NRP] nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (Art. 43) The Court heard addresses by Mrs. - the Agent of the German Government (‘the Government’), the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicant on the need for a written procedure. The applicant informed the Registrar on [DATE_TIME] that he would not be filing a memorial. The President gave the applicant’s lawyer leave to use the [NRP] language in the proceedings (Rule 27 § 3). The Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court (Rule 50). The hearing was held in public in [LOCATION], [ LOCATION], on the appointed day. The applicant, a national born in Horkheim, was involved in a road accident. According to the police report (Verkehrs-Ordnungswidrigkeiten-Anzeige), he had attempted to overtake a car, although the traffic situation was unclear. The result had been a collision which caused damage to both vehicles. When he was questioned, the applicant made the following statement: “I was wearing a crash helmet when the accident occurred; I was not injured.’” The Court ordered the applicant to pay a fine of £10,000 to the German government. The applicant refused to pay the fine and the case was dismissed. Mr. [PERSON] was fined DM 125 for “joint responsibility for a road accident due to overtaking in an unclear traffic situation such that a collision was caused with another road-user’ The decision was based on section 24 of the Road Traffic Act (Strassenverkehrsgesetz - see paragraph 38 below) The driver of the car was likewise fined for a “regulatory offence“. The court informed the applicant that it intended to discontinue the proceedings as they were time-barred and order costs against the Treasury. The applicant would have to bear his own necessary costs and expenses (notwendige Auslagen) Heilbronn Police Authority took a decision to impose a fine (Bussgeldbescheid) on the defendant for a breach of the Road Traffic Regulations. The defendant appealed against this decision. By an order made on [DATE_TIME], the public prosecutor’s office in [LOCATION] forwarded the case to the Heilbronsen District Court for a decision. After the case had been submitted, prosecution of the ‘regulatory offence’ became time-barred under section 26(4) of [ LOCATION]. The proceedings must therefore be stayed by reason of there being a technical bar to prosecution (Verfolgungshindernis) Heilbronn Regional Court dismissed the appeal (sofortige [PERSON) as being unfounded. The court held that Article 6 § 2 (art. 6-2) of the Convention did not apply to the case. Mr. [Person] had himself admitted to the police that he was not expecting the car which was moving out to the left onto the road in front of him to make a U-turn. He had consequently attempted to overtake it but had been unable to avoid a collision despite his efforts to brake. In such circumstances it would have been unjust to award the defendant’s necessary costs and expenses against the Treasury, especially as the prosecution had become time-barred only during the court proceedings. The decisions of the District Court and the Regional Court did not offend the presumption of innocence, says the Constitutional Court. ‘The decision not to order the Treasury to pay the costs and expenses of the party concerned obviously cannot be regarded as a punishment (Bestrafung) or even be equated with such,’ says the court. success. But the decision as to costs and. expenses does not make any finding that the person concerned is guilty: it derives. merely from the suspicion falling on him, which had given rise to his being prosecuted for. a ‘regulatory offence’ The decision is therefore rightly confined to the finding that. the defendant would most probably have been found guilty.

The investigation was into whether any person had benefited from theft or false accounting, contributing to the resources of a proscribed organisation or from contraventions of betting regulations. The maximum penalty for failure to attend an interview was [DATE_TIME] imprisonment or a fine not exceeding GBP 5,000. The applicant's solicitor sent a letter to the financial investigators indicating that the applicant's replies could become admissible evidence at a trial and suggesting that the purpose of the interview was to compel him to disclose his defence. The interview did not take place and the applicant was convicted of this offence in the Magistrates' Court and fined the sum. Belfast County Court allowed the applicant's appeal against conviction, finding that the prosecution had not proved the absence of a reasonable excuse. The judge noted that the Northern Ireland Court of Appeal had dealt with a similar case which related to the same legislation and the same investigation. The only outstanding matter was whether the applicant should have attended the interview and then refused to answer questions, or, as he did, refuse to attend the interview once he failed to receive the assurances he had asked for. The application was heard by a judge at Belfast Crown Court who found in favour of the applicant. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38544/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged, inter alia, that the first applicant's right to remain silent and not to incriminate himself had been breached in criminal proceedings against him. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Court decided to communicate to the respondent Government both applicants' complaint about the lack of a prosecuting authority before the Vorarlberg Independent Administrative Panel. The Government filed observations on the admissibility and merits. This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section. The applicant, Mr [PERSON], was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION]. The Bregenz District Authority (Bezirkshaupt-mannschaft) served an anonymous order (Anonymverfügung) upon the applicant in the sum of 800 [NRP] schillings (ATS) It stated that the driver of the car, registered in the applicant's name, had exceeded the city area speed limit of 50 km/h by 21km/h. The applicant did not comply with the anonymous order. Consequently, the order became invalid (see paragraph 31, below) The applicant appealed to the Vorarlberg Independent Administrative Panel. The Panel dismissed the applicant's defence, noting that the University of Texas had 14 different locations in [LOCATION]. The Panel observed that the information provided by the first applicant had indeed been inaccurate. The applicant was not prosecuted for exceeding the speed limit. He was ordered to pay ATS 180 by way of contribution to the costs of the appeal proceedings. He raised various issues regarding the tribunal quality and the fairness of the proceedings. However, given that the relevant sentence of section 103 § 2 of the Motor Vehicles Act has the rank of constitutional law, he did not raise the issue of his right to remain silent and not to incriminate himself.

name: John Beard
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case originated in an application lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention by two [NRP] nationals. The applicants alleged that planning and enforcement measures taken against them in respect of their occupation of their land in their caravans violated their right to respect for home, family life and private life. They further complained that they were subject to discrimination as gypsies. The Commission declared the application admissible on [DATE_TIME]. The Grand Chamber determined that the case should be decided by the Grand Chamber. The applicants and the Government each filed a memorial. Third-party comments were also received from European Roma Rights Centre. Mr Makarczyk, who was unable to take part in further consideration of the case, was replaced by Mr [PERSON] (Rules 24 § 5 (b) and 28) The applicants are gypsies by birth. They regard themselves as being [LOCATION] folk. As they wanted to set up a family site, in [DATE_TIME] they bought a piece of land. The site is 0.365 hectares in area, and is positioned in the countryside between the motorway and the [ LOCATION]-Carlisle railway line. The applicants applied for planning permission to build a small close-knit gypsy family site for six. They were prosecuted in Lancaster Magistrates' Court for being on the land unlawfully. The Government disputed this assertion, stating that local authority records indicate that it was after the applicants had occupied it that complaints were received about its condition. The applicants' planning application was refused on the grounds of adverse effect on highway safety and impact on visual amenity. On [DATE_TIME], the applicants submitted an appeal to the Secretary of State for the Environment. These appeals were heard by an Inspector appointed by the secretary of state. In his report, the Inspector stated inter alia: “9. Policy 6 seeks to limit development of land in the open countryside to that needed for the purposes of agriculture and forestry, or other uses appropriate to a rural area” The appearance of 6 caravans on the site would cause serious harm to the character of the landscape and be in conflict with Policy 14, even allowing for the proximity of the site to [LOCATION]. ... By all accounts the land was overgrown until [DATE_TIME] or thereabouts; it is not overgrown now. The hedges along the lane obstruct the visibility at bends, alterations in the hedge line would be a help but in my view such alterations would not go far towards improving the overall situation. ... Cinderbarrow lane and its junctions with the main roads clearly have hazards for traffic. Lancashire Council appeal site to be used by gypsy caravans. Council say they have made adequate provision for gypsies in the area. Council says they have added 14 additional residential pitches and 4 pitches for touring carvans. The Council's own site at [LOCATION] has 20 double pitches and can, therefore, accommodate 40 gypsy cars. The appeal judge says he finds the implications for highway safety to be so unacceptable as to warrant a refusal of permission. He says there is a special need for accommodation to be provided for gypsy people. The decision has been made to deny the appeal and the appeal has been upheld. The applicants were offered places on an authorised site, which they turned down for strong personal reasons. The applicants did not appeal against this decision to the High Court, as such appeals can only be made on limited grounds. In my view the special need for accommodation to be provided for gypsies is not so weighty in the present case as to outweigh the harm caused to the character of the area. ...” The time period for compliance was extended to [DATE_TIME]. The Inspector also revoked the condition of returning the land to its former condition finding it excessive due to the tidying work carried out by the applicants. The applicants applied for planning permission for a smaller gypsy site which would consist of one mobile home and a transit pitch. The application was refused and they appealed against this decision. On [DATE_TIME], the appeal was dismissed again, on grounds of visual amenity and adverse effect on highway safety. The current level of authorised provision within the district is 100 caravan pitches of which 20 pitches are on a council-owned site. The applicants were advised by the police to stay away from the area. The use of the site for the stationing of a caravan and the addition of a second would “seriously harm the character and appearance of the surrounding area”. The applicants were convicted of failing to comply with the enforcement notice and were fined GBP 300 plus costs. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, inter alia, endorsing the judge's finding that: “Subsection 3 [of the Town and Country Planning Act] is not concerned with the policy issues as arise in relation to the circumstances in which gypsies live” The case was remitted to the Crown Court judge, who took the view that there was ‘powerful mitigation’ and sentenced the applicants to a fine of GBP 150 and GBP 100 costs. It would have been more appropriate to commence civil injunctive proceedings in the County Court. The first applicant made an undertaking to the Court to remove his caravans from his land and to break up the hard surface laid out on the land by [DATE_TIME] The applicants applied for a variation of the undertaking, seeking an extension of the time for compliance as they had been unable to find anywhere else to site their caravan. The application was refused and the applicants were ordered to pay the Council's costs. In order to avoid committal and the ensuing deleterious consequences on the first applicant's health, the applicants vacated their land and are currently without a fixed address. The Government submitted that 12 vacancies arose on [LOCATION], the official site in the area. There were 99 caravans on seven authorised private sites, where there were 31 vacant pitches. The applicants stated that these sites are largely seasonal for tourists and that gypsies were not welcome. Only one of them has been designated as official gypsy site but is still inhabited mostly by non-gypsies. This site had 40 pitches. There was a waiting list but the applicants would only have had to wait [DATE_TIME] for a vacancy to occur. There were a further 107 private authorised/touring and residential sites, comprising, respectively, 4,834 and 561 pitches, with substantial numbers of vacancies.

The applicants alleged that planning and enforcement measures taken against them in respect of their occupation of their land in their caravans violated their right to respect for home, family life and private life. The Commission declared the application admissible on [DATE_TIME]. The applicants and the Government each filed a memorial. Third-party comments were also received from the European Roma Rights Centre. The applicants are gypsies by birth. The site is 0.365 hectares in area, and is positioned in the countryside between the [LOCATION] motorway and the [ LOCATION]-Carlisle railway line. When the applicants bought it, they stated that it was generally regarded as being an eyesore. They referred to it as ‘an eyesore’ and said it was a ‘disturbing’ building. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the Government’s use of the site was an ‘abhorrent’ act. The applicants applied for planning permission for a small close-knit gypsy family site for six people. They were prosecuted in Lancaster Magistrates' Court for being on the land unlawfully. The Government disputed this assertion, stating that local authority records indicate that it was after the applicants had occupied it that complaints were received about its condition. The applicants' planning application was refused, by letter, on the grounds of adverse effect on highway safety and impact on visual amenity. On [DATE_TIME], the applicants submitted an appeal to the Secretary of State. The appeals were dismissed. The site is in an area of open countryside, it is undulating pasture land with a few buildings in the locality and can be seen. The appearance of 6 caravans on the site would cause serious harm to the character of the landscape. [The first applicant] proposed to plant hedging along 3 of the boundaries and he has already done some of this. The types of hedging which are characteristic of the area would not provide much in the way of screening for [DATE_TIME], [the applicant's] approach is to plant quick growing conifers but I share the Council's view that these are not in keeping with the character. ... Cinderbarrow lane and its junctions with the main roads clearly have hazards for traffic. The hedges along the lane obstruct the visibility at bends. Lancashire Council says the appeal site is not in line with its development plan. Council's own site has 20 double pitches and can accommodate 40 caravans, it says. Council says gypsy accommodation has been made over and above that which led to the area being designated. Council say gypsies have been provided with 14 additional residential pitches and 4 pitches for touring carvans on 4 private sites. The Council says it has also provided 4 private pitches for the use of its own site. The appeal hearing continues, with the appeal hearing continuing until the appeal is heard again on February 6. The hearing continues and the appeal continues. The aim is to provide land for caravan sites for gypsies within, or close to, the main urban areas. There are 5 permanent gypsy sites in [LOCATION], including the one at [ LOCATION]. The County Council are actively pursuing the provision of 3 further sites, none of which are in [ LOCATED] The applicants did not appeal against this decision to the High Court, as such appeals can only be made on limited grounds. They were offered places on an authorised site, which they turned down for strong personal reasons, namely, since this particular site was occupied by a large, violent gypsy family who had attacked them on more than one occasion. The time period for compliance was extended to [DATE_TIME]. The applicants applied for planning permission for a smaller gypsy site. The application was refused and they appealed against this decision. On [DATE_TIME], the appeal was dismissed again, on grounds of visual amenity and adverse effect on highway safety. The applicants were advised by the police to stay away from the area. The use of the site for the stationing of a caravan and the addition of a second would “seriously harm the character and appearance of the surrounding area”. The current level of authorised provision within the district is 100 caravan pitches of which 20 pitches are on a council-owned site. In total, there are an average of 29 vacancies on private sites and 7 on the council owned site. The applicants were convicted of failing to comply with the enforcement notice and were fined GBP 300 plus costs. Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, inter alia, endorsing the judge's finding that: “Subsection 3 [of the Town and Country Planning Act] is not concerned with the policy issues as arise in relation to the circumstances in which gypsies live” The case was remitted to the Crown Court judge, who took the view that there was “powerful mitigation” and sentenced the applicants to a fine of GBP 150 and GBP 100 costs. The applicants were directed by the judge that they had no alternative but to plead guilty as they did not have a defence to the charges. The first applicant made an undertaking to the Court to remove his caravans from his land and to break up the hard surface laid out on the land by [DATE_TIME]. The applicants applied for a variation of the undertaking, seeking an extension of the time for compliance as they had been unable to find anywhere else to site their caravan and due to the first applicant's ill health. The application was refused and the applicants ordered to pay the Council's costs. The second applicant submitted in an affidavit to the County Court that they had made continuous and strenuous enquiries but had been met with refusals – letters from 22 sites were enclosed. There were space for 99 caravans on seven authorised private sites. The applicants stated that these sites are largely seasonal for tourists and that gypsies were not welcome. The total number of unauthorised encampments in the area had almost doubled from 11 to 21. The conditions on this site were closely monitored by [DATE_TIME] inspections by a resident warden. This site had 40 pitches. There was a waiting list but the applicants would only have had to wait for a vacancy to occur. There were currently 31 vacant pitches and a further 107 private authorised/touring and residential sites, comprising, respectively, 4,834 and 561 pitches.

The Court heard addresses by Mr [PERSON] and [Person]. The Court declared the application admissible after a hearing on [DATE_TIME] (Rule 59 § 2). As he risked being declared bankrupt before his tax liability had been determined by the courts, he also requested a stay of execution in respect of the amounts assessed. The Tax Authority responded by saying that the prerequisites laid down in section 49, subsection 1(2) or (3), of the Tax Collection Act [Uppbördslagen, 1953:272] had been fulfilled. The Tax Authority finds that the applicant's ability to pay is open to serious doubt. The Tax Authority is of the opinion that [the applicant] has to provide security for the amount ... in respect of which he has requested a stay of execution. Should you fail to provide. security by the date mentioned above, the Tax Authority will reject your request.” The applicant, who did not furnish security, lodged a notice of appeal. The applicant appealed to the Svea Court of Appeal, claiming that the District Court's decision amounted to a violation of Article 6 of the Convention. The appeal was dismissed. Leave to appeal against the appellate court's decision was refused by the Supreme Court. The amounts relating to income tax did not become payable until [Date_TIME]. The matters were automatically referred to the County Administrative Court for determination. The bankruptcy proceedings were terminated owing to a lack of assets. The County Administrative Court upheld the Tax Authority's decisions of 22 and 27 [DATE_TIME] and rejected the applicant's request for an oral hearing. It considered that there had been sufficient reasons to impose the surcharges in question and that no legal basis for remitting them had been shown. The applicant alleged that the statutory notices were invalid on grounds of fraud and illegal conspiracy. The Sheriff Court upheld the council’s claim, rejected the applicant's counter-claim and found that the case did not meet the criterion for referral to the Court of Session. On the latter date, the motion to this effect was granted by way of interlocutor. This was done when the first defenders, despite their defence, served the applicant with a notice of proceedings. First defenders failed to apply for a hearing. train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on [DATE_TIME.
